Here's the puzzle. In 2016–2025 the play-by-play tags about 20 fake punts a season
across the whole league, 0\.9% of punt-formation snaps, and they picked up a first
down 63% of the time.[^fakes] Fake field goals have nearly disappeared: about
3 a season tagged in 2016–2025, against about 12 a season
in 1999–2005. If fake punts convert more than half the time, why don't coaches call them more?

1. **They work *because* they are rare.** The conversion rate is high because coaches choose the
   moment: a look they scouted, a return team turned to set its wall, a short distance. Call fakes
   every week and return teams play punt safe every week, and the rate collapses. This is game theory
   in its plainest form: the right number of fakes is small but not zero, so that the other side has
   to respect the possibility.
2. **The downside is lopsided.** A punt from your own 35 gives the opponent the ball somewhere around
   its own 25, while a failed fake gives it the ball at your 35, 40 yards closer, often with momentum
   and a home crowd behind it. A coach can survive a punt; he gets second-guessed for a week over a failed fake.
3. **The personnel aren't built for it.** The punt team is backups, linemen and specialists. A
   punter's pass and a personal protector's run are plays the unit practices a few minutes a week.
4. **Analytics took the edge off.** Fourth-down models now tell coaches to *go for it* in the open,
   with the offense on the field, in many of the situations where a fake used to be the only way to
   try. Why risk a trick with backups when you can run your best short-yardage play with starters?

Fakes also reveal the deeper logic of the kicking game. Every punt-team formation is an offensive
formation, with the same eligible receivers as any other: the two ends of the line and everyone
lined up off it. A player wearing a lineman's number (50–79) can still be one of them, but only if he
reports to the referee before the play, who announces it to the defense; that is how a reserve tackle
caught a touchdown in the film room below. And every return team is a defense that has to decide what
it fears. When a punt team lines up, the return team is reading it, and vice versa, just as on any other
down.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Ravens 2012–2024, Justin Tucker and the 66-yard kick"}
For most of his 13 seasons in Baltimore, Justin Tucker was the standard for accuracy: he made
89\.1% of his 468 regular-season field-goal attempts.
His most famous kick came on **September 26, 2021, at Detroit**. Baltimore trailed 17–16 with no
timeouts; a fourth-and-19 completion got the ball to the Lions' 48, and with three seconds left
Tucker tried a 66-yarder, two yards longer than any field goal ever made. It hit the crossbar, bounced
up and over, and Baltimore won 19–17.[^tucker66] **What to notice:** the arithmetic (a snap from the
48 plus 18 yards is 66), the venue (indoors at Ford Field, no wind), and the operation: snapper Nick
Moore and holder Sam Koch had to be perfect for a kicker to swing that hard. Tucker made
22 of 30 in 2024. Baltimore released him in May 2025, the league suspended him for
ten weeks that summer, and he was still unsigned when the 2026 season began.[^tuckerout]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cowboys 2023–2025, Brandon Aubrey and the moving range line"}
Brandon Aubrey took the long way to the NFL: a first-round pick of Toronto FC in the 2017 MLS draft,
then the USFL's Birmingham Stallions, then a contract with Dallas in July 2023. He made the first 35
field-goal attempts of his NFL career, a record, and in 2024 he made 14 field goals of 50 yards or
more (in 17 tries), the most in a season in NFL history.[^aubrey] By the end
of 2025 he had made 6 from 60-plus yards. **What to notice:** how a kicker like
that changes the coach's decisions. In 2023–2025 35% of Aubrey's attempts came
from 50 yards or more, against 24% for the league as a whole. For Dallas,
field-goal range started near the opponent's 42, so a drive that stalled at midfield still had a
reasonable shot at three points, and fourth-and-long near the 40 became a kick instead of a punt.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Jaguars 2025, Cam Little goes to 68"}
On **November 2, 2025**, at Las Vegas, Jacksonville's second-year kicker Cam Little ended the first
half with a **68-yard field goal**, breaking Tucker's record by two yards (the Jaguars won 30–29 in
overtime). In Week 18 he made a 67-yarder at home against Tennessee, the longest ever kicked in an
open-air stadium.[^little] **What to notice:** the setting of the record (the dome at Allegiant
Stadium, no wind) and the season it came in, the first with teams breaking in their own kicking balls.
Little made 30 of 34 field-goal tries in 2025; the 60-plus-yard kick, a stunt a
decade ago, had become a planned weapon at the end of a half.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks, NFC Championship (2014 season), the fake that won a conference"}
On **January 18, 2015**, Seattle trailed Green Bay 16–0 in the third quarter of the NFC Championship
Game and lined up for a field goal at the Packers' 19. Holder Jon Ryan, the punter, took the snap,
sprinted to his left, away from the rush, and threw a 19-yard touchdown pass to Garry Gilliam, a
rookie offensive tackle wearing No. 79 who was playing the wing and slipped out of the formation
unnoticed.[^seafake] Seattle went on to win in overtime. **What to notice:** the holder already has
the ball in his hands; a wing is off the line, so he is a back and an eligible receiver, and a
player wearing 79 there must have reported to the referee, a detail a block unit sending everyone
at the kick can easily miss; and nobody stayed home to cover him.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Dolphins and Colts, two direct-snap fake punts"}
The fake punt in this chapter's figure, a direct snap to an up-back running through the middle, is
the bread-and-butter version, and it works when the return team isn't looking for it. In the AFC
Wild Card game at Pittsburgh on **January 8, 2017**, Miami, down 17 in the second quarter, faced
fourth-and-1 at its own 41. The snap went straight to safety Michael Thomas, who ran up the middle for
three yards and a first down.[^miafake] For the opposite lesson, find the Colts' fake punt against
New England on **October 18, 2015**. Most of the punt team shifted to one side; wide receiver Griff
Whalen became the snapper and safety Colt Anderson lined up behind him. The play was meant only to
draw the Patriots offside, but Whalen snapped the ball anyway, and Anderson was dropped for a
one-yard loss (with an illegal-formation flag the Patriots declined). It is remembered as one of the
worst fakes ever run.[^colts] **What to notice:** a fake needs surprise *and* a sound formation; the
Dolphins had both, the Colts had neither.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the range finder"}
**On every fourth down, call it before the offense lines up: go, punt or kick.**

- **Do the arithmetic.** Line of scrimmage plus 18 is the kick. Under 40 yards: a kick is nearly
  automatic. 50–55: depends on the kicker and the day. Beyond 58: only for a special leg, a roof or
  thin air, or the end of a half.
- **Check the conditions.** Roof open or closed? Flags on the uprights (and which way they blow
  for *this* end)? A cold night? Did the broadcast show the kicker's warmup line?
- **Read the distance and the score.** Fourth-and-1 at the opponent's 38 is a go in most modern
  playbooks; fourth-and-8 at the same spot is a kick for a good kicker, a punt for a shaky one.
- **When the punt team trots out, look at the return team.** Two vices on each gunner and a
  deep returner: a return. Seven or eight on the line, crowding one side: a block. Defenders on the
  field, corners in tight on the gunners, no one turning back: punt safe, they fear a fake.
- **Watch where the punter aims.** From midfield, a high pooch toward the 10 and gunners racing to
  the spot. From deep, a directional kick to the numbers.
- **Then watch the returner's hands.** One arm waving above the helmet is a fair catch. A
  returner backing away from a ball inside his 10 is letting it go for a touchback. Listen for the
  officials sorting out who touched it first.
:::

**How long is the kick, and what should the coach do?**

**It's a 55-yarder (37 + 18), four yards beyond this kicker's line into the wind: punt, or go for

40°F, kickers made 41% of their tries from 55 yards and beyond, and those were the
hand-picked long kicks coaches chose to attempt in the cold; this one is also into a 15-mph wind. The cost of a miss is
the spot of the kick, the opponent's 45, a short field in a tied game.

Between the other two options it's close, and teams differ. NFL offenses converted
39% of fourth-and-6 plays in 2016–2025, and a failed try hands the opponent the ball at its own 37. A punt from the 37 is
the pooch scenario from the heatmap: into the wind it won't carry into the end zone, so the punter can
aim high at the 10 and the gunners can down it. A conservative coach punts and plays for field position
in a tied game; an aggressive one goes for it. The kick is the one choice the conditions rule out.

**Return, block or safe? And what should the punt team's personal protector do about it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A punt block, overloading the punt team's right side.** The tells: eight on the line instead of the
usual six, five of them on one side, and only one vice per gunner (strictly, a single "jammer"), because the return team needed the
extra bodies up front and doesn't care much about the coverage if it gets a hand on the ball. A team
setting up a return would have two vices on each gunner and players ready to peel back for a wall; a
punt-safe team would have defenders, not rushers, and nobody committing this many players to one side.
(A side note on the rules: the limit of six defenders on one side of the snapper applies only to
field goals and tries, not to punts.[^fgrules6]) Eight on the line is a strong tell, not a guarantee:
return teams sometimes show exactly this overload and then peel back into a return at the snap.

The personal protector's job is exactly this moment. Before the snap he calls out the overload and
slides the protection toward it, so the shield (the wings and the PP himself) and the right-side
blockers take the inside rushers and
the outermost man is left with the longest path. The punter may also take a slightly quicker drop or
angle his kick away from the overload. The trade for the return team: with one vice per gunner, a punt
that gets off cleanly will meet gunners arriving fast, so expect a fair catch. Fourth-and-9 from the 31
isn't a fake situation, so the punt team just punts, quickly.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Add 18.** A field goal is the line of scrimmage plus about 8 yards to the holder and 10 for the end
  zone. *Field goal range* is a coach's judgment about this kicker today, weighed against going for it
  and punting, and a miss costs the spot of the kick.
- **Kickers are far better than they were**, so range has moved out about five yards in a generation.
  Wind and cold shorten it; altitude and roofs lengthen it. The data understates bad weather's effect,
  because coaches don't try the kicks they expect to miss.
- A field goal is a **1.3-second snap-hold-kick operation** behind a wall that steps inside and must not
  give ground. Block units overload, crash the middle and aim at the block point; the rules ban
  leaping, covering the snapper and more than six rushers on one side.
- The **2015 extra-point change** turned a 99% kick into a roughly 94% one and made the kick and the
  two-point try worth almost the same, so two-point tries doubled and the choice now follows the score.
- A punt is **protect, kick, cover**. The NFL's base is the spread punt, with the wings and personal
  protector forming the shield in front of the punter; only the gunners may release before the kick,
  so two vices on each gunner is the return team's first priority. Judge punts by **net** and by where the opponent starts, not by gross distance.
- The return team chooses before the snap: **return, block or safe**. The rules of the loose ball
  (fair catch, touchback, first touching, muff versus fumble, kick-catch interference) all follow from
  one question: who touched it first? Fake punts succeed more often than not precisely because they are
  rare.

[^weather]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2010–2025. Indoors = `roof` of "dome" or "closed"; outdoors = "outdoors" or "open". The same pattern shows elsewhere. Indoors, kickers made 69% of their 50-plus-yard tries and outdoors 63%, while 50-plus kicks were 20% of attempts indoors and 16% outdoors.
